title: INTEGRATING GENERATIVE AI INTO PROGRAMMING EDUCATION: AN EXPLORATORY STUDY OF STUDENT INTERACTIONS AND LEARNING OUTCOMES
extended_summary:
This doctoral thesis examines how undergraduate students interact with ChatGPT in an introductory programming course and how different instructional approaches shape those interactions, learning outcomes, and student perceptions. The central problem is that while generative AI tools are increasingly used in programming education, there is limited empirical evidence on how pedagogical design influences whether students use these tools productively, reflectively, or dependently.

The study implemented three AI integration strategies across three in-class practice sessions during a semester: unguided ChatGPT use, explicit instruction on effective prompting, and structured scaffolding through a lab guide with sample prompts. Quantitative data included a prior knowledge test and post-session quizzes/post-tests, while qualitative data included 2,388 ChatGPT prompts and student reflections. The analysis identified several student-AI interaction profiles, including AI-Reliant Code Generators, AI-Reliant Code Generator & Refiners, AI-Assisted Code Refiners, AI-Collaborative Coders, and AI-Independent Coders.

The population consisted of 158 undergraduate students at Middle East Technical University in an introductory programming course. The intervention took place in in-class practice sessions, indicating a classroom-based implementation within a single university context in Turkey. The study focused on how prior programming knowledge and instructional condition related to students’ prompting behavior, performance, and experiences with ChatGPT.

The main conclusions are that pedagogical design strongly affects how students engage with generative AI. Explicit instruction and scaffolding shifted interaction patterns and reduced purely solution-seeking use relative to unguided use. Students with lower prior knowledge were more likely to depend on ChatGPT for direct answers, while stronger students used it more reflectively for revision and improvement. Performance improved significantly following explicit instruction, and student perceptions evolved from emphasizing convenience and accessibility toward valuing learning support and personalized assistance. However, challenges remained, including misinterpretation, limited feedback quality, and overreliance, underscoring the importance of instructional mediation and AI literacy.
quality_tier_rationale: This is an exploratory mixed-methods thesis with quantitative post-tests and qualitative log/reflection analysis, but the provided text does not indicate random assignment, a strong quasi-experimental comparison design, or full reporting of effect sizes and validity details. It therefore fits a correlational/qualitative evidence level with limited causal credibility.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports significant improvement in programming performance after explicit instruction and meaningful shifts in interaction patterns, but effect sizes are not reported and several findings are qualitative or mixed, including concerns about overreliance. Impact is therefore promising but unclear in magnitude.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT was integrated into an introductory undergraduate programming course across three instructional conditions—unguided use, explicit instruction on effective prompting, and structured scaffolding—to support code generation, revision, debugging, and conceptual explanation during in-class practice.

finding.finding_summary: In a mixed-methods study of 158 undergraduate students in an introductory programming course, post-session quiz results indicated significant performance improvement following the explicit instruction condition, suggesting that prompt-writing training and AI literacy improved programming-task performance. The abstract reports statistically significant gains but does not provide exact effect sizes, confidence intervals, or standard deviations in the provided text.
finding.measure: Prior knowledge test and post-session quizzes on introductory programming tasks

finding.finding_summary: The study identified multiple student-AI interaction profiles from 2,388 ChatGPT prompts, ranging from 'AI-Reliant Code Generators' to 'AI-Collaborative Coders' and 'AI-Independent Coders,' showing that pedagogical design shaped how reflectively students used ChatGPT. Students with stronger prior knowledge tended to use the tool for refinement and improvement, while lower-knowledge students were more likely to depend on direct solutions, indicating both support for metacognitive strategy use and risk of dependency; no effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Thematic analysis of ChatGPT prompt logs and classification of AI interaction profiles; student reflections

finding.finding_summary: Qualitative reflections suggested students’ perceptions evolved over time from valuing accessibility and convenience toward valuing learning support, task progress, and personalized assistance, implying improved engagement and perceived usefulness. However, students also reported challenges including misinterpretation, limited feedback, and overreliance, so the affective/experiential outcomes were not uniformly positive.
finding.measure: Student reflections on experiences using ChatGPT across three sessions

finding.finding_summary: Students initially emphasized ChatGPT’s accessibility and convenience, and qualitative findings indicate the tool supported task progress and personalized assistance during in-class programming activities. These results suggest productivity and workflow benefits, although the study did not report direct time-on-task or workload metrics, so operational gains are inferred from self-reported experience rather than quantified efficiency outcomes.
finding.measure: Qualitative reflections about accessibility, convenience, and task progress while using ChatGPT
